newsitem.title: NORWAY: E.Timor activists win Peace Prize, Indonesia angry.
newsitem.headline: E.Timor activists win Peace Prize, Indonesia angry.

text.p: Two East Timor independence campaigners were awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday in a decision which immediately angered the territory's ruler, Indonesia.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee, sharply criticising Indonesia which invaded the territory in 1975, said the award to East Timor Bishop Carlos Belo and resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta was aimed at influencing the drawn-out conflict there.

The prestigious award, which confirmed the committee's ability to fuel controversy, was welcomed around the globe, including by former colonial power Portugal, the Vatican, and neighbouring Australia. But it was greeted with hostility by Indonesia.
"This was about to become a forgotten conflict and we wanted to contribute to maintaining the momentum," Committee chairman Francis Sejersted told reporters at the Nobel Institute in Oslo.
"We do hope there is a message (in this award)...to the Indonesian government to change its policy."

Indonesia reacted angrily to the award with Foreign Ministry spokesman Ghaffar Fadyl calling Ramos-Horta, 48, a "political opportunist". He avoided comment on Belo, 50, East Timor's outspoken and often fiery Roman Catholic bishop.

"It is quite a surprise and quite regrettable that such a reputable institution has decided to give this prize to a person like Ramos-Horta, who has quite clearly been involved in the manipulation of the people of East Timor for his own interests," Fadyl told Reuters.
East Timor has bedevilled Indonesia's international relations since its troops invaded the eastern half of Timor island in late 1975 when Portugal left after 400 years.
Indonesia annexed the territory that is located in the Timor Sea, about 500 kms (300 miles) north of Australia.

"In the years that followed it has been estimated that one-third of the population of East Timor lost their lives due to starvation, epidemics, war and terror," the Nobel committee said in a statement, publicly accusing Indonesia of oppression.
The United Nations refuses to accept Indonesia's claim to East Timor and still regards Portugal as administering power.
It has brokered regular meetings between Indonesia and Portugal and started an intra-Timorese dialogue but progress has been painfully slow. The next meeting is due in December.
But diplomatic and political analysts said it would be hard for the Indonesian government to swallow the decision and could even delay peace efforts.
"It's a difficult decision for Indonesia," a diplomatic source in Indonesia told Reuters.
"In a sense it represents the acknowledgement of the international community that Indonesia's claims to successful integration (of East Timor) haven't been accepted."
There was also concern that hardliners in Indonesia could see the award as proof of their fears of an international conspiracy against their country.
Belo, who was saying a Mass in a school in the East Timor capital Dili when the award was announced, spoke of peace and reconciliation.
"I see it as a victory for East Timorese...and all Indonesians," he told Reuters. "Peace can be achieved through non-violent means," he added.
Ramos-Horta, a U.S. educated lawyer who fled to Australia three days before the invasion, had a mixed reaction.

"I'm happy but surprised, because Bishop Belo deserves the Nobel Peace Prize but the other person who should be sharing the award with him is my leader, Xanana Gusmao," Ramos-Horta told Reuters from his mother's home in Sydney, Australia.
Gusmao is serving a 20-year jail sentence in Indonesia.
